extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of satire/classical literature; scholars of Rabelais; humorists studying comic devices
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and employing comic devices characteristic of Rabelaisian Renaissance satire: grotesque bodily humor, mock erudition, bawdiness, verbal invention, and institutional parody in dialogic narrative. Useful for authors or analysts seeking to reproduce or analyze this comedic mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: grotesque_bodily_imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Use vivid, often violent or animalized bodily metaphors and images to provoke shock-laughter (e.g., 'The gnawings of my stomach... make it bark like a mastiff'; references to flaying, plucking skin, trotter-pies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy exaggerated physical sensations, animal comparisons, and visceral detail to produce comic disgust/amazement; juxtapose bodily realism with rhetorical commentary. Example passages: 'gnawings of my stomach... bark like a mastiff'; discussion of being 'flayed' by a wife. Anti-pattern: euphemising too much — the humor here relies on blunt, concrete bodily language.

rubrics_metrics.name: bawdy_sexual_double_entendre
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of sexual innuendo, explicit sexual imagery, and double meanings for comedic effect (e.g., 'She will suck me at my best end', 'intercrural pudding', repeated erotic references framed as innocent statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine faux-serious exposition with explicit or suggestive sexual phrasing so that the literal/figurative readings collide. Use euphemism and crude directness alternately for surprise. Warning: humor depends on audience tolerance; too clinical or too coy reduces effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: mock_scholarly_parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody of learned registers and authorities by invoking philosophers, historians, legal texts, and pseudo-scholarly citations in absurd contexts (e.g., invoking Pythagoras, Socrates, Bartholus, Propertius to justify comic assertions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimic academic tone and citation to lend ludicrous authority to trivial or obscene claims. Use formal references as comic contrast to subject matter. Example: 'Bartholus, Lib. 5. de Verb. Oblig.' used amid burlesque narrative. Anti-pattern: sincere erudition without ironic contrast loses the parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: institutional_and_religious_satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirize religious/monastic practices by literalizing or reinterpreting rituals, rules, and titles (e.g., 'De missa ad mensam', 'Holy Chapel' = convent kitchen, fasting to noon, matins of nine lessons linked to appetite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose institutional absurdities by treating rituals as mundane logistics or bodily necessities. Use specific, recognizable practices so the parody reads as targeted critique. Examples in text show how ritualized language applied to food and appetite yields satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: bathos_and_high_low_contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Create comic effect by applying high, elevated diction or classical allusion to low, bodily, or vulgar subjects (grand phraseology about bread, oracles, philosophers applied to dungeries, pisseries, porridge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an elevated tone while describing trivial or obscene details to produce anticlimax (bathos). The sharper the stylistic mismatch, the stronger the comic effect. Avoid flattening both levels into the same register; contrast is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: piling_and_catalogue_listing
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ long lists and paratactic series (often morphologically playful) to accumulate comic momentum: 'they dunged in the dungeries, pissed in the pisseries, spit in the spitteries...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition, parallel forms, and escalating lists to overwhelm the reader and convert monotony into humor. Repetition of form with varying content produces rhythm and surprise. Overuse without variation can become tedious.

rubrics_metrics.name: absurd_similes_and_unexpected_juxtapositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage wildly incongruous similes/metaphors and catalogued odd items to create surreal comedy ('a sot, a pot, a fool, a stool, a winter mitten, a truckle for a pulley...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juxtapose incongruous objects and images to surprise readers and highlight absurdity. Use rapid-fire unrelated comparisons to create a comic cumulative effect. Keep specificity — odd concrete items make the image funnier than vague abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: dialogue_driven_timing_and_interruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic pacing arranged through tight dialogic exchanges, interruptions, asides, and character retorts (quick back-and-forth among Panurge, Epistemon, Pantagruel, Friar John).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on snappy interjections, abrupt exits, and contradictory takes between characters for comedic rhythm. Let characters embody differing comic stances (the gullible, the pedant, the bawdy jokester). Timing — short retorts and sudden capitulations — produces laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: verbal_invention_and_neologism
rubrics_metrics.description: Coin and adapt words, morphological play, suffixation, and mock-technical terms for comic color (e.g., 'nine-lecture-powdered labourer', 'salmigondinois', 'nockandroe').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent words by blending registers, languages, or suffixes to create playful lexical surprises. These neologisms often reveal character voice or satirize pedantry. Ensure invented terms remain comprehensible in context or deliberately opaque for grotesque effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: misinterpretation_and_reinterpretation_comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive humor from conflicting readings and willful reinterpretations of prophecies, signs, or texts (Panurge and Epistemon offer wildly different takes on the sibyl's octastich).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up ambiguous material (prophecy, proverb) and exploit divergent interpretations by characters; let self-interest, pride, or desire bias readings for comic irony. The audience perceives the gap and enjoys the equivocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: ritualized_performance_and_stage_gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic stage business and physical ritual: the sibyl's spindle-acts, apron-over-head like a priest's amice, throwing verses into the air, burning laurel that makes no crackle — performative absurdity as humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid stage actions and ritual mockeries to make the scene theatrically ridiculous. Nonverbal detail (gestures, props, costume mimicry) emphasizes parody of solemn ceremonies. Visualized gestures strengthen comic imagery in prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: refrain_and_formulaic_repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use repeated formulaic phrases and refrains ('Let us go', 'Farewell, Friar John', 'By the hook of God') to establish comic rhythm and character habitus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic repetition creates running jokes and expected punchlines; vary or break the refrain for surprise. Overuse can dull effect; the comic value often comes from timing and slight variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: prophetic_ambiguity_and_oracular_parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody prophecies and oracular methods (sycamore leaves with metred lines, ritual burning, non-crackling laurel) to expose vagueness and arbitrary interpretation as comic devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame divination as elaborate but ultimately vague ritual; highlight randomness (leaves scattered by wind) and the human tendency to read meaning into chance. The text's octastich and its multiple plausible readings illustrate the device.

rubrics_metrics.name: appeal_to_authority_as_comic_device
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoke canonical names and textual authorities to absurd ends (citing Propertius, Tibullus, Porphyrius, Herodotus to justify folk omens or a jack-pudding's acting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authoritative names to satirize appeals to learned opinion: over-citation lends mock-seriousness and exposes pretension. Best used when the citation is disproportionate to the claim, producing irony.
